data.title: Hunter Biden says Joe Biden's cancer is spreading: 'It's very debilitating'
data.description:
Former President Joe Biden’s cancer has spread to other parts of his body, his son Hunter Biden revealed in an interview, describing the disease as “very painful” and “very debilitating.”

“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” he told the BBC’s “Newsnight” Friday. “It’s really sad to watch.”

Several months after leaving the White House, the former president announced in May 2025 that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer. At the time, his office said the cancer appeared to be “hormone-sensitive,” allowing for “effective management.”

Hunter Biden became emotional during the interview while discussing his father’s condition, saying that watching the former president’s health decline has been “really hard.”

“The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good,” he said.

Despite the cancer’s progression, Hunter Biden said his 83-year-old father remains active and engaged in public life.

Former first lady Jill Biden said in a June “The View” appearance that, while things have “slowed down” for her husband since his diagnosis, he is still keeping busy.

Aside from a memoir slated to come out around the November midterm elections — and a late July controversy surrounding leaked audio files appearing to show the former president sharing classified information with a ghostwriter in 2016 and 2017 — former President Biden seldom weighs in on the current political landscape.

In June, however, he delivered a speech a Democratic Party Gala in Maryland — swiping at President Trump’s multiple Washington D.C. renovation projects.

“It’s not just his vanity projects … putting his name on the Kennedy Center. Building an arch in his own honor. Even hiring his own pool guy to fix the reflecting pool,” the former president said. “Whoa, what a loser.”

“He’s still doing his thing,” Hunter Biden said during Friday’s BBC interview. “He so believes in this country.”

Hunter Biden also reflected on his father’s infamous June 2024 debate performance against President Trump, saying he felt “shocked” while watching from home in California.

“I knew something was wrong,” he said of the debate.

Hunter Biden said his father remains at the “center of our family” as he undergoes treatment, calling the former president the “best father, the best husband, the best grandfather.”

data.title: Maher says Trump further left than Dems citing Intel stake: 'This is socialism'
data.description:
Comedian Bill Maher accused President Trump of openly embracing “socialism” more than Democrats, as democratic socialism is on the rise in the U.S.

In a Friday segment on “Real Time,” Maher said Republicans were hypocrites when it came to accusing democratic socialists of being communist, especially the Trump administration.

“It’s so interesting, the wrinkle in this story, because now that they’re communists, there’s an opening for socialism. And you know who’s filling it? Donald Trump,” he said. 

Maher called out the Trump administration’s stake in Intel, Nvidia and Nippon Steel, saying “we basically run their boardroom now.”

Trump said in April that federal stock holdings in Intel generated more than $30 billion over the last several months, after he authorized the U.S. government’s investment in the struggling semiconductor chip manufacturing company last summer.

“It’s like, what? The president is just singling out a huge CEO of an important company and so they had to scramble the Jets and have a meeting at the White House and what happened at the end of that meeting? Okay, you say we get 10% of your company. That is thuggish behavior,” Maher said.

The decision garnered support from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) but drew pushback from Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) called it a “terrible idea” and a “step toward socialism.”

“If socialism is government owning the means of production, wouldn’t the government owning part of Intel be step toward socialism?” he wrote on social media.

“And you know this is socialism, I think, because Bernie Sanders agrees with it all. He wants to do it with the AI companies,” Maher continued.

Trump has likened democratic socialism to communism in remarks made to reporters in the Oval Office in June. 

Candidates affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have been winning elections across the country.

“I think it’s the biggest threat to our nation there is, maybe since our founding,” he continued. “That includes World War I, World War II, September 11, it includes the Pearl Harbor attack.”

“We have never seen anything like this in modern time,” Maher concluded about Trump’s government stake.

data.title: Miller saga muddles midterm landscape for Ohio GOP
data.description:
The controversy around Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) is complicating the midterm landscape for Ohio Republicans as Democrats build momentum in the Buckeye State, a former battleground that’s become a red state in the Trump era.

Miller, who is running for a third term in a competitive House district, is facing calls to step down after allegations of domestic abuse toward his ex-wife, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). He has forcefully denied the claims, but the controversy could make his red seat an easier pick-up opportunity for Democrats in the high-stakes fight for House control. 

Ohio is also host to a highly competitive Senate race, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) has lodged a comeback bid against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R) that could bolster Democrats’ chances of taking back the upper chamber this fall — plus a neck-and-neck race for Ohio governor in the state that’s been GOP-led for more than a decade.  

“In an environment where Republicans have been particularly strong in Ohio, this year’s environment is going to be much more challenging for them, and this certainly doesn’t help things,” said Robert Alexander, a political science professor at Bowling Green State University in Ohio, on the Miller developments. 

“I think that the fact that so much of the attention is on Republicans is a good thing for Democrats,” he added. “The more it’s about Republicans, I think the better that Democrats will likely do.”

Miller has denied allegations from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, in a New York Times report last week that the Ohio lawmaker scalded her chest with hot water, held a gun to her head and fractured their daughter’s collarbone, among other allegations. The pair divorced in 2025 and have since been locked in a bitter custody battle over their daughter. 

The House Ethics Committee announced Monday that it’s investigating allegations of domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use after Miller said he has “nothing to hide.” 

Miller also said that he received a Monday phone call from President Trump, who told him that it would be a tough race and that he didn’t know whether the embattled lawmaker would be able to pull it off in the fall. The House Republican said he drew comparisons to the president’s own controversies on the 2016 campaign trail, signaling his intent to stay in the race. 

But a new co/efficient polling memo released this week showed Miller down 14 percentage points against Brook Park City Council member Brian Poindexter, the Democrat nominee for the typically red 7th Congressional District. 

“The district is Republican, but it’s not so heavily Republican that a Democrat could never win,” said Justin Buchler, an associate professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland.

Now, a chorus of Capitol Hill Republicans are calling for Miller to resign ahead of an Aug. 10 deadline that would let the state GOP pick a replacement nominee for the November ballot. 

Bernie Moreno, the senator and Miller’s former father-in-law, said the congressman needs “serious psychological help.” Husted, in the middle of his must-win Senate fight, said Miller needs to “step aside as a candidate” and resign.

Democrats are also signaling that the Miller controversy could become a liability for the GOP in other House races.

“Every single vulnerable Republican who has coddled and stood by these creeps should be ashamed of themselves,” Democrats’ House campaign arm spokesperson Viet Shelton said in a statement.

Mehek Cooke, an Ohio Republican strategist, told The Hill that Miller has become “an unnecessary distraction” as Republicans head into a highly competitive midterm year. She shrugged off the latest polling, but called for Miller to step aside. 

“Republicans should take this race seriously [and] put forward candidates who reflect our values and keep the focus on delivering results,” Cooke wrote in an email. 

Buchler drew parallels to the controversy that built around Democrat Graham Platner’s Senate bid in Maine until the progressive bowed to calls from party leaders to withdraw. 

“There came a point at which it was just too much,” Buchler said of the pressure on Platner. 

If Miller does stay in the race, “then you have a candidate who is, in some ways, damaged by the allegations, and in some ways damaged by political leaders in the state coming out against him,” Buchler said. “If he does step down, then you have the question of who fills the vacancy.” 

In response to an inquiry about the Miller saga, House Republicans campaign arm’s spokesperson Zach Bannon projected confidence without directly namedropping the embattled lawmaker. 

“Ohio’s 7th congressional district is a Republican seat that strongly backed President Trump and consistently rejects the radical left’s agenda. It will remain red this November,” Bannon said. 

As the Miller saga unfolds, the stage is set for highly competitive races for the Senate and governor’s mansion that could mean Democrats gain ground in the red state. Once considered a purple national bellwether, Ohio has grown increasingly red since siding with Trump in each of his three presidential elections — but experts say that could change. 

“Ohio leans Republican, but it is not a solidly Republican Deep South state,” Buchler said. “This is a midterm, which means that elections nationwide are going to move towards the party out of the White House, that’s the Democrats. That could, in principle, mean that Democrats pick up some wins in states like Ohio.” 

Brown, a major recruit for Democrats, has pulled slightly ahead of Husted in Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) polling average of the Senate race, which prognosticators consider among just a handful of toss-up contests that could determine the upper chamber’s majority.

Term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine (R) last year appointed Husted, then the lieutenant governor, to temporarily fill Vice President Vance’s old seat in the Senate. The Senate contest is a special election to fill out the remainder of Vance’s term, which runs through 2028. 

In the governor’s race, DeWine has endorsed Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur and former co-leader at Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), to succeed him. But Ramaswamy lacks elected experience and, as a first-generation American, faces headwinds from some anti-immigrant voters in the GOP.

He faces a tough rival this fall in Democrat Amy Acton, a former Ohio health director who worked with DeWine during the pandemic. Cook Political Report last month shifted the governor’s race toward Democrats, into the toss-up column. 

“It is a coin flip for both the governor’s race and the Senate race. I wouldn’t be surprised if both of those races were within the margin of error, ultimately,” Alexander said. 

At the same time, Ohio is also home to a handful of competitive House races that could give Republicans new pickup opportunities under newly redrawn, GOP-friendly maps.

Democratic Reps. Marcy Kaptur and Greg Landsman are both running in reshaped districts, Cook rates as “toss up” and “lean Democrat” contests, respectively. 

Ohio GOP consultant Matt Dole attributed the Rust Belt state’s highly competitive environment in part to Trump fatigue — as the president weathers lackluster approval ratings, and frustration over his handling of the economy and the war in Iran — and to a “general fatigue” with Republicans in a state where the party has dominated every statewide partisan office since 2010. 

Republicans are still feeling bullish about their midterm chances this cycle, Dole said, “but it is certainly the most competitive we’ve seen in the last 20 years.”

data.title: Are Republicans blind to the canaries in the Florida and Texas coal mines?
data.description:
I have never understood how self-proclaimed or anointed election experts, who are wrong time and again, remain the go-to experts for much of the media. What I do understand is why they are wrong so often.

Many of these experts live in bubbles quite removed from Main Street America and especially the working-class voting population.

To be sure, Republicans have more than their fair share of the snobbish, pompous and the ignorant, living happily and hedonistically within those same bubbles of luxury that will never be attainable to many of their fellow Americans. 

Having grown up in poverty myself, I can say that most in the working-class do not resent others’ success.  They just want those who do attain or are handed that success to understand and address the plight of the disenfranchised and the powerless if they ever do find themselves in positions of power.

In my time, I have known many paycheck-to-paycheck parents and voters, many of whom still deeply believe in President Trump. And yet all say their paychecks buy less and less with each passing month.

My wife and I have done all right in life. But of late, every single time she comes back from the grocery chain store with just two small bags of items, she points out the ever-increasing prices.  This is no one’s imagination. This is reality.

Some in the administration will claim until the cows come home that the stock market is doing great; 401(k) accounts are growing; and all of our rich friends are getting richer. But one truth for one class does not cancel out the quality-of-life crushing truth for another.  

Politics, like much of life, is cyclical.  Democrats used to be really good at addressing bread and butter issues. Then Republicans cleverly hijacked that winning formula. And now, it seems to be swinging back toward the Democrats.

As we rapidly approach the midterms in November and the 2028 presidential election, history and reality are working against the Republicans. History reminds us that in 20 of the last 22 midterm elections, the party not occupying the Oval Office gained ground. That, coupled with the reality of more and more working class Americans struggling economically, should be a five-alarm warning for Republicans.

Yet, so many seem blissfully oblivious to it all.

As an example, I offer up the red states of Florida and Texas. Maybe the warnings are not reaching certain ears in the administration and the Republican leadership, but I well-connected Republicans in those two states are increasingly worried about the Senate race in Texas and the governor’s race in Florida. 

Aside from their concerns that the Republican Party is coming down on the wrong side of bread and butter issues, they worry that they are putting up flawed candidates in a midterm that already favors Democrats.

In Texas, a new Fox News poll shows Democratic senate candidate James Talarico (D) leading Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by 3 points. And among “extremely motivated voters” from both parties, Talarico’s advantage in the race grows to 6 points. Even worse, one-quarter of non-MAGA Republicans support Talarico. All this in a state Trump won by 14 points in 2024.       

Why? One reason is that Republicans are wasting time and money attacking Talarico’s personal life. Another is Ken Paxton’s personal flaws. A third is that working-class Texas feels shunned by Republicans promoting what is supposed to be a great economy based on 401(k) performances.

A similar situation exists in Florida. Every Republican I speak to in that state believes term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) to be “the best governor in the nation.” Many also believed that his wife Casey would have been a lock to replace him, but we will never know. President Trump, as is his prerogative, endorsed Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) before the Republican primary for governor had even begun. The primary is still coming up, but Donalds will be the Republican nominee.

In the meantime, he is getting pounded by negative attack ads that will be used against him by the eventual Democratic nominee (most likely former Republican Congressman David Jolly, now a Democrat) this fall. Florida Republicans I know are nervous.

That, once again, comes on top of real economic pain felt by every paycheck-to-paycheck voter.  Karl Rove, who driving force behind George W. Bush election as president, has warned that “Republicans risk making the same political mistake he believes cost Democrats the 2024 election, arguing the party is relying too heavily on favorable gross domestic product and job figures while failing to address the economic pressures many voters still feel.

Even as Democratic Socialists of America gain ground with outright communists winning nominations, a multitude of “canary in the coal mine” examples exist on the Republican side as well, including in Florida and Texas. If both of these flawed canddates fail, the Republican Party is in deep trouble.

I am no expert, but if I were the Republican leadership, I might be trying to figure out how to get some emergency oxygen to these canaries before it is too late. 

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

data.title: Maher rips Paul for publishing Fauci diaries: 'Your entire brand is Senator Right to Privacy'
data.description:
Comedian Bill Maher ripped Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) for his ongoing scrutiny of Anthony Fauci’s time as White House chief medical adviser, arguing the senator strayed from his libertarian roots by releasing the former health official’s diary and pushing to hold him in contempt of Congress.

“Stop threatening to put everyone in jail who you just don’t like,” Maher said Friday on HBO’s “Real Time with Bill Maher.”

“Rand babe, your entire brand is ‘Senator Right to Privacy,’” he continued. “You’re the libertarian guy, the Fourth Amendment guy.”

Maher’s comments came days after the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, chaired by Paul, voted 8-5 to refer Fauci for contempt of Congress after he repeatedly refused to answer questions during a hostile Senate hearing last week about the COVID-19 pandemic.

Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right 111 times during his testimony before the committee, where Republicans slammed his response to the pandemic and blamed him for the public’s declining trust in the American healthcare system.

Ahead of the hearing, Paul released more than a thousand pages of Fauci’s notes that he kept on his government computer to the public, referring to them as Fauci’s “COVID diaries.” The records included the former medical adviser’s conversations with administration officials during the early months of the pandemic.

Maher argued that Paul releasing Fauci’s private notes was difficult to reconcile with the senator’s reputation as one of Congress’s most vocal critics of government intrusion.

“It’s your family legacy. Your entire political career has been about warning us about government overreach,” Maher said, referring to former Rep. Ron Paul — a Texas libertarian and Rand Paul’s father.

“You printing someone’s diary is like AOC wearing a gown that says tax the poor,” Maher added, joking about Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (D-N.Y.) controversial appearance at the 2021 Met Gala — where she donned a dress reading “Tax the Rich.”

Fauci received a sweeping pardon from former President Biden on his last day in office in 2025. The pardon covered potential federal offenses between Jan. 1, 2014, and Jan. 19, 2025.

data.title: RFK Jr. visits CDC Atlanta office one year after fatal shooting
data.description:
Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. visited the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta on Friday, one year after a shooting forced the facility to lockdown and resulted in the death of a police officer.

Kennedy attended the memorial event to honor the life of DeKalb County Police Officer David Rose. The event was open to employees of the agency, and he later held an in-person fireside chat.

“Today, we honored Officer David Rose’s extraordinary courage, service, and sacrifice by dedicating a memorial roadway and plaque in his memory, ensuring his legacy will continue to inspire all who enter the CDC campus,” Kennedy wrote in a social media post.

The shooting occurred Aug. 8, 2025, when a gunman opened fire outside the CDC building, killing Rose who was a responding officer. Officials said almost 500 shell casings were recovered, and about 200 struck six facilities on the agency’s campus.

Authorities said they found documentation in the alleged shooter Patrick Joseph White’s house, expressing his discontent with the COVID-19 vaccinations. 

Kennedy was not named in any documentation found, though he has been criticized by Republicans and Democrats for his decision-making regarding funding cuts for mRNA research and firing members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP).

He also received a letter from Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) that called for the secretary to fire Robert Malone from the ACIP. Malone, a Kennedy appointee, less than 48 hours after the attack, made a blog post that included images of guns and memes with the words “if you need a disarmed society to govern, you suck at governing.” 

Malone is a former researcher who helped lay the groundwork for mRNA vaccine technology, but has since turned into a self-professed anti-vaxxer.

During the in-person fireside chat Kennedy hosted on the eve of the shooting, he allegedly praised the scientist’s work at the agency but also called for greater scrutiny of scientific findings.

“You can’t just trust a scientist, because scientists have biases, too,” he said, according to a transcript of his 43-minute chat obtained by The Washington Post. “They’re all hoarding their own data.”

data.title: Iran signals Strait of Hormuz deal close, but ceasefire dispute lingers
data.description:
Iran announced Saturday that it is nearing an agreement with Oman over control of the Strait of Hormuz but warned that its reopening would depend on other conditions, including compensation from the U.S. to Iran.

The emerging deal would establish a new framework for managing traffic through the critical shipping corridor, where Iran has restricted traffic and targeted vessels in response to the U.S.-Israeli strikes that began the war on Feb. 28, 2026.

“Iran and Oman are close to an agreement on the legal framework and management of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday. “However, reopening the Strait depends on other conditions, including U.S. remedy for violations of the Islamabad understanding.”

Araghchi stated that the previously established designated routes for shipping vessels traveling through the strait were no longer acceptable to Iran.

Iran and Oman are instead discussing a temporary route while they work through the technical and legal issues surrounding a new system, Araghchi said, adding that naval and military talks between the two countries are also underway.

A U.S. official told Reuters on Friday that the Trump administration would lift its blockade of Iranian ports once a final deal restoring commercial shipping “without impediments” was announced.

“As always, U.S. actions will continue to be performance-based and tied to Iran’s implementation of its commitments,” the official said.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard, however, stressed Saturday that reopening the strait depended on a separate agreement with the U.S., and not simply a deal with Oman.

“Whenever the United States accepts Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will certainly be reopened,” spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said, according to Reuters, citing Iran’s Tasnim news agency.

Dangers to vessels in the strait continued Saturday, when a ship was struck by an unknown projectile near Khasab, Oman, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center.

The strike sparked a fire that was later extinguished, and the vessel and its crew were reported to be safe.

data.title: Ex-GOP strategist: 'This might be the year' Democrats win Texas
data.description:
Former GOP strategist Joseph Moreno said “this might be the year” that Democrats win in Texas after a three-decade drought since a Democrat has won in the Lone Star State.

In an appearance on CNN’s “The Lead,” host Jake Tapper asked Moreno about recent polling that showed Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D-Texas) leading Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) 47 percent to 45 percent.

“It surprises me, and it worries me a little bit, Jake. Normally, I would say, ‘I’m not worried about this,’ right? It’s been 30 years since a Democrat won statewide office in Texas,” Moreno said.

Paxton won a primary runoff against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) earlier this year with the help of an endorsement from President Trump.

Talarico won the Democratic primary against Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D) in March and received heavy support from Democratic leadership including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

“The problem is, here’s what happens — in 2024, the Republican was up by 2 percent, wins by 8 percent. In 2020, Cornyn was up 10 percent, wins by 10 percent,” Moreno continued. “Now, you’ve got Talarico even, or maybe even ahead of Paxton. Paxton is so flawed. I’m embarrassed as a Republican.”

Paxton faced scrutiny from Texas state officials following a state House investigation that found he had “used, misused, or failed to use his official powers in a manner calculated to subvert the lawful operation of the government.”

He also was impeached by the Texas House, faces 20 charges of misconduct in office, previously faced three felony securities fraud charges and had an extramarital affair.

A Texas Pulse/Texas A&M Bush School poll released Friday had 47 percent of likely Texas voters planning to support Talarico, while 43 percent chose Paxton.

“I hate to say it, this might be the year for Democrats in Texas,” Moreno concluded.

The general election between Paxton and Talarico happens on Nov. 3.

data.title: What happens when progressives stop reproducing?
data.description:
The U.S. General Social Survey has tracked American life since 1972. Its findings reveal a pattern that political consultants have largely ignored.

The deep division in national politics is no longer an ideological battle over tax codes and foreign policy. Rather, it’s a battle of the bedrooms. Left-leaning Americans are averaging far fewer children than conservatives, whose birth rates hold steady near the 2.1 replacement level.

Evolutionary demographers Martin Fieder and Susanne Huber recently pinpointed the precise moment this divergence began. For Americans born before 1943, political leanings showed little correlation with family size. The baby boom was an equal-opportunity event. But for those born after 1943, political ideology became a reliable predictor of family size.

As the researchers note, higher education accelerates this divide. Women now earn 58 percent of all bachelor’s degrees, and university campuses tilt heavily toward progressive politics. This extended academic timeline delays marriage, trading early family formation for career building. The campus functions as an ideological funnel, leaving the highest-scoring students on standardized tests with the lowest reproductive rates. Academics have engineered a bizarre biological paradox: the most credentialed segment of society is choosing genetic extinction, leaving the future to the children of subcultures that skip the university pipeline entirely.

Political parties invest billions in media campaigns to win over independent voters. Demography operates by simple math, counting the actual humans entering the world. Frequent religious attendance remains the primary engine of conservative fertility. Churches provide strong social infrastructure, offering communal childcare, moral validation, and structured matchmaking. In such an environment, raising four children changes from an expensive luxury hobby into an absolute cosmic obligation.

This reproductive advantage compounds over generations through family retention. Pew Research Center data confirms that children raised in highly religious, conservative households overwhelmingly maintain those exact beliefs into adulthood. Ideology functions like a heritable trait. When a culture passes down both its metaphysical worldview and its high-fertility habits, it unlocks exponential demographic interest. The devout always claim that Jesus saves, but in this specific instance, he also populates.

Progressive philosophies face no dramatic defeat at the ballot box. They require no cancelation by rivals and no losses in public debate. They are simply running out of citizens. A political movement that fails to reproduce automatically surrenders its institutional real estate to the descendants of the people who fill church pews instead of university lecture halls.

Conventional political analysts obsess over changing party platforms and legislative gridlock. The real driver of history is a profound divide in foundational attitudes toward permanent obligations. One mindset treats cultural continuity as life’s primary goal. The alternative prioritizes personal autonomy, geographic mobility, and self-definition above generational replacement.

Fieder and Huber isolate these metrics with rather unsexy statistics. Decades of low birth rates systematically warp the age profile of a nation. Roads, bridges and power grids built for a growing society become impossible to maintain when the tax base shrinks. Domestic economies become structurally addicted to foreign immigration to keep factory floors running and eldercare facilities staffed.

National debates focus on quarterly productivity figures, economic slowdowns and media polarization. Meanwhile, the biological reality of reproduction runs in the background. Differential reproduction operates completely outside the 24-hour news cycle. Certain belief structures maintain compatibility with biological survival over centuries, while others act as demographic sterilizers. Societies survive political volatility quite easily; they do not survive long-term reproductive deficits.

Building a nation of genuine worth requires citizens to view family formation as a primary objective. This outlook belongs almost exclusively to traditional communities that view children as central duties rather than limits on personal freedom. Macro-level cultural shifts are merely the sum of millions of private decisions, including the mattress-testing ones, made over decades. By the time a nation notices its declining birth rate, the concrete has already set.

The survival of any political philosophy relies on its submission to basic reproductive reality. American economic dominance requires a baseline population to secure domestic supply chains, staff military branches and drive innovation.

This continuity relies on a classic form of conservatism — entirely distinct from populist trends or immediate election cycles — built on the absolute conviction that a society has a duty to reproduce itself. It demands a mindset that rejects the idea of a terminal generation, viewing children as an existential necessity and the ultimate justification for a nation’s existence.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

data.title: How does cyclospora compare to some of the worst outbreaks in US history?
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Amid the ongoing investigations into outbreaks of both “explosive diarrhea”-causing cyclospora and salmonella affecting dozens of states, the daily headlines are reminiscent of past foodborne illness crises that gripped the nation.

As of August 4, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported that there have been 10,468 lab-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis since May 1, including those tied to Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce sourced from Mexico.

The CDC says there have been more than 12,255 unconfirmed cases, many of which were reported in Michigan, where two people have died.

Meantime, jalapeño peppers – also sourced from Mexico – have been linked to at least 345 cases of salmonella across 27 states. At least three dozen people have been hospitalized, with the outbreak prompting major Mexican food chains Chipotle and Qdoba to pull jalapeños from their menus.

Despite the widespread publicity and thousands of cases involved, the two current outbreaks have so far proven less deadly than some historic, notorious cases.

Contaminated oysters lead to typhoid outbreak (1924)

Oysters contaminated with Salmonella Typhi led to a deadly outbreak of typhoid fever in 1924 that killed 150 people and sickened an estimated 1,500, according to Michigan State University researchers.

Those who died may have been ill for up to three weeks, left “delirious or lying motionless from exhaustion, eyes half closed in what is called ‘the typhoid state,'” according to one report.

The tainted oysters were believed to have been distributed by a company in West Sayville, New York. It was the deadliest outbreak in U.S. history and led to the creation of National Shellfish Sanitation Program.

Mexican-style cheese (1985)

The outbreak, centered in Los Angeles County, was believed to have been caused by tainted, unpasteurized milk used to make soft Mexican cheese.

Of the 142 cases, more than half were pregnant women or their children. According to a report in the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), 28 people died, including 18 adults and 10 newborns.

Investigators ultimately traced the outbreak to cheeses made by Jalisco Mexican Projects Inc.

Jack in the Box (1992-1993)

An outbreak of E. coli killed four children in four states and sickened more than 700 people across Washington, Idaho, California and Nevada before investigators finally traced it to undercooked hamburgers sold at Jack in the Box.

The ensuing investigation by federal regulators changed regulatory practices in the U.S., experts say.

An investigation by the CDC identified five slaughter plants in the U.S. and one in Canada as the likely sources of animals used in the contaminated lots of meat and identified potential control points for reducing the likelihood of contamination. The animals slaughtered in domestic slaughter plants were traced to farms and auctions in six western states. No one slaughter plant or farm was identified as the source.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture mandated a Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point system, which helps identify and control hazards within the system of food production. The system provided for more monitoring and controls to rapidly limit the spread of outbreaks.

Schwan’s ice cream (1994)

A nationwide salmonella outbreak that sickened an estimated 224,000 people in 1994 was caused by ice cream from Minnesota-based Schwan’s Company.

Investigators determined that the source of the salmonella was the tanker trailers that transported the pasteurized ice cream premix. Those same trailers previously carried non-pasteurized liquid eggs that tested positive for the bacteria, according to a study published by the National Library of Medicine.

E. coli outbreak in spinach (2006)

A 2006 outbreak of E. coli traced to contaminated fresh spinach infected 199 people across 26 states, according to the CDC. Three people died, including a 2-year-old.

After speaking with patients, some of whom still had the spinach bags in their homes, federal investigators identified the source of the contamination as a load of spinach grown on a field in California adjacent to land used for cattle grazing, according to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Samples of river water taken as close as one mile away from the spinach were found to be contaminated with E. coli, as were samples of cattle and wild pig feces from the ranch.

Peanut butter (2008-09)

Peanut butter tainted with salmonella killed nine people and sickened hundreds, leading to a 28-year prison sentence for the former CEO of the Peanut Corporation of America, Stewart Parnell.

An indictment said the company misled its customers about the existence of salmonella in its product, even when lab tests showed it was present. It added that the co-workers even fabricated certificates accompanying some of the peanut shipments saying they were safe when tests said otherwise.

A jury convicted Parnell of 71 counts including conspiracy, obstruction of justice, wire fraud and other crimes related to the salmonella outbreak in 2008 and 2009.

It prompted one of the largest food recalls in U.S. history.

Contaminated cantaloupes (2011)

Two farmers were charged and convicted in a listeriosis outbreak that left 33 dead and sickened another 147, according to the CDC.

The tainted cantaloupes came from Jensen Farms in Holly, Colorado.

The owners of the farmer, Eric and Ryan Jensen, were accused of failing to wash the melons properly, leading to the nationwide outbreak. They were both given five years of probation.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.
